2: Here are Part 2's three gates on one page.
The least privilege gate is done when every high-privilege grant is justified or removed, and every Tier 1 app registered in your own tenant has a workload Conditional Access policy.
The conversion gate is done when converted identities sign in without stored secrets, and the legacy accounts are disabled after a clean parallel run.
The lifecycle gate is done when the owner change, orphan, review and decommission paths have all run and left records.
Each gate names the read-only kit checks that prove it, and each has a rollback.
Every identity has an owner, a sponsor, a reason and a target.
Each one is retired, moved to a managed identity, or given a certificate or a federated credential.
And none holds a password that never expires, or is left without an owner.
3: Least privilege applies to software too, and a workload can use its access faster than any person.
The guide cuts privilege in five places.
Prefer delegated permissions where a user is present.
Judge each grant by its type, not its name, because Mail Send as an application permission is critical.
An application permission reaches across the whole tenant.
And removing a permission from the app doesn't revoke the grant, so revoke it on the enterprise app too.
No standing privileged role unless the record justifies it.
A privileged service principal is a control-plane asset.
Third, Azure roles, scoped to the one resource a workload uses.
Fourth, custom security attributes, so Conditional Access can pick apps by fact.
Fifth, workload Conditional Access, with real limits.
It covers only single-tenant apps, never managed identities, and only when each one is assigned directly.
And new grants go through the tiered approval.

It reads app roles, delegated grants, directory roles and Azure roles for each service principal.

The plan has three writes: two app role removals and one narrowed grant.
Each removal goes through the resource, never the app, and nothing is sent until a reviewer approves the plan's hash.
The eighth chapter keeps the two workload policies as reviewed files, one per ring.
Every policy is created in report-only mode.
Ring two isn't, because one workload signed in from outside its known networks.
Enforcement waits for the see-so's decision and a reviewed sign-in summary.

sis-uh's baseline requires that only administrators register apps, that user consent is restricted, and that an admin consent workflow is in place, so keep the ScubaGear report.

6: Conversion follows the Federal Modernization Workbook's Book 02's fourth phase.
It takes six to eight weeks, and the order is a managed identity first, then a federated credential, then a certificate.
A federated credential must be tested with a real token exchange.
Step two names two human owners and a rotation schedule.
Step three runs old and new side by side for thirty days.
The application uses the new identity, and the old account stays enabled.
Watch the new identity's sign-ins in Entra, and the old account's logons on the domain controllers.
Step four disables the old account, but never deletes it.
An Active Directory account moves to a holding container.
A secret is removed only after the new credential has carried real traffic.
Step five records the result: the target, the date, and the disabled object's I D.

9: A service account's events come from its owning system and from credential expiry, not from H R.
The one exception is the sponsor.
When an owner leaves or changes roles, the transfer starts at least ten business days ahead.
Make it a step in that person's H R mover and leaver workflows, so nobody has to remember it.
An app with no named owner is an orphan.
It becomes Tier 1, the governance office takes it over, and there are thirty days to find an owner or start retiring it.
On day thirty-one, access is suspended.
An A I agent is disabled as soon as the finding is confirmed, because an agent can act.
Inactivity is a second orphan signal, from a preview report of each service principal's last sign-in.
And owners review their app's permissions every quarter, with at least two owners per app where possible.
10: Retirement always disables first, so nothing breaks silently, and deletes later.
An Active Directory account is disabled, and its service principal names are removed only after the observation period.
New tokens stop at once, but tokens already issued stay valid until they expire.
A deleted app can be restored for thirty days.
A service principal is blocked from signing in to this tenant.
If it's deleted and restored, its Conditional Access policies don't come back.
A managed identity loses its role assignments first, and once deleted, it can't be recovered.
An agent can be disabled by its sponsor, but not re-enabled.
Deleting a blueprint removes its agents too.
Every deactivation shows in the audit log.
File that entry with the decision.
11: The workbook's tenth chapter turns this gate into a scheduled run.
Each run compares every identity with a baseline that someone approved by its hash.
On the second fixture day it finds seven ownerless orphan candidates, and two apps unused for over ninety days.
It finds three accounts whose password never expires, and three credentials added outside the pipeline.
A credential counts as the pipeline's only when two separate records agree.
The review check finds an app whose last owner review was in May, too long ago.
Then each run is packaged with a checksum for every file, chained to the day before.
So a swapped package or a missing day shows up as a break.
The period report is what the I S S O receives.
Here the chain is unbroken, but the period isn't complete.
Orphans and passwords that never expire are still open.

13: sequel Server follows the same logic, with three kinds of principal.
The engine's service account works only while Active Directory is in charge.
It only changes what Entra I D and Azure see.
The instance's own Entra identity is a managed identity on sequel Server 2025, with no credential at all.
On sequel Server 2022 it's an app registration with a Key Vault certificate, which needs a named renewal owner.
Application logins move from sequel passwords to Entra logins: a managed identity first, then a certificate, and a secret only as a documented exception.
And the same thirty-day parallel run applies.
A renewed certificate that nobody uploaded fails at expiry, so automate the upload.
And on an Arc server, every allowed process presents the same identity, so treat one login per server as the unit of attribution.
14: A I agents follow this guide, with a few additions from Book 17.
Every agent needs a sponsor when it's created.
The blueprint holds the credentials, so one action on the blueprint reaches every agent made from it.
Ordinary users can't create blueprints, and a production handshake comes before any agent goes lyve.
No production blueprint holds a secret, and every A P I key is recorded as an exception.
Access comes through packages with end dates, so a sponsor who does nothing lets access expire.
The agent platform has been generally available since April 2026, with a partial subset in G C C. Agent Conditional Access is still in preview.
The workbook's ninth chapter checks all of this, and here it finds twenty-two findings, four of them top priority.
For G C C High and D O D, Microsoft has published nothing, so govern the service principals the agents run as.

16: Every app owner can add a credential and act as the app, so keep owners to the two people who configure it.
Disabled isn't revoked, because issued tokens stay valid, so in an incident, also remove the credentials.
A privileged service principal is a control-plane asset, not an ordinary app.
Workload Conditional Access silently skips managed identities, multitenant apps, and anything assigned through a group.
And by default, whoever builds an agent becomes its sponsor, so close blueprint creation and set the sponsor on purpose.
